t: Ibn Khaldun wrote it in 1377 as the introduction to a universal history, and it came to be regarded as an independent work in his own lifetime.
It sets out a new science of human society, ʿilm al-ʿumrān, and explains the rise and fall of dynasties through ʿasabiyyah, or group feeling.
It was received without much enthusiasm for centuries, first printed in Cairo in 1857, and translated into French in 1863 and English in 1958.
dyk: Ibn Khaldun wrote that when officials were questioned about armies, or the goods of the wealthy were assessed, the true figures would be found to amount to a tenth of what those people had said.
ev: Ibn Khaldun completes a draft of the Muqaddimah at Qalʿat ibn Salama
The Muqaddimah is printed at the Bulaq Press in Cairo in a standalone volume
Étienne-Marc Quatremère prints the Arabic text in three volumes in Paris
The complete Ottoman Turkish translation is published, in 1860 or 1861
William McGuckin de Slane publishes a French translation in three volumes
Franz Rosenthal publishes an English translation

f.made: Ibn Khaldun, who wrote it at Qalʿat ibn Salama after withdrawing from political life, as the introduction and first book of his planned world history, the Kitab al-ʿIbar
f.form: An Arabic treatise in six books on society, politics, urban life, economics and knowledge, with discussions of historiography, theology and the natural sciences; the Kitab al-ʿIbar it introduces fills seventeen volumes of 500 pages each in its modern edition
f.where: Read in printed editions and in translations into Ottoman Turkish, French and English; manuscripts copied in Ibn Khaldun's lifetime survive, some with his own marginal notes or additions
f.known: The ʿasabiyyah cycle of dynasties; the new science of ʿumrān; a criticism of the errors of historians; the contrast of nomadic and sedentary life; passages on taxation and prices; the discussion of alchemy
